newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour warned it must raise taxes if elected.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour warned it must raise taxes if elected.

text.p: As Britons voted on Thursday, the Labour party received another warning that it would have to raise taxes if -- as opinion polls suggest -- it takes power after 18 years in opposition.
American Express Bank said Britain was set for faster longer-term economic growth, but ambitious targets set both by Labour and the Conservatives for curbing public spending were unlikely to be met.
"Tight spending plans are probably not achievable," American Express senior economist Trevor Laugharne said in a report on Britain's economic prospects.
"By European standards, the UK has a low tax burden...which will almost certainly have to be raised during the coming parliament."

The warning was the latest in a series from leading economic bodies, including the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which said last month that Britain needed an early increase in interest rates and some fiscal tightening to restrain demand.
Opinion polls gave Tony Blair's Labour party a clear lead over Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives.
Labour has pledged iron control of the public finances, no increases in income tax and a tough inflation target of 2.5 percent or less.
The American Express study noted that Britain's tax burden was 35.75 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), down from a peak of 39.75 percent in 1994/95.

It said Conservative spending plans over the next few years, which Labour is committed to living within, envisaged a real rise in spending of no more than 0.6 percent per year -- a level not achieved for generations.
"This 'low' rate of spending appears when demands for additional resources are increasing and will be politically difficult to reject," Laugharne said.
Labour is committed to improving funding for health and education, although it argues that much can be achieved by efficiency gains and re-allocating existing resources.
Many economists say Gordon Brown, who would be Chancellor of the Exchequer in a Labour government, faces an early dilemma if he takes over the Treasury on Friday.
The Bank of England has been pressing for higher interest rates since last December, arguing that early warning signals such as money supply growth point to a pickup in inflationary pressures.

But British exporters are already suffering because of the strong pound, which makes their goods more expensive abroad, and raising interest rates from the present 6.0 percent could boost the pound further.

"A new chancellor, unpacking his briefcase tomorrow in number 11, Downing Street, faces the rather unpalatable prospect of either rising interest rates very quickly or raising taxes in a mini-budget beyond what he has already said he would do," said David Philpotts, an economist at Schroders.
Philpotts told Reuters Financial Television that Brown could win credibility with financial markets with an early rate rise.
However, other analysts were unconvinced.
"I think Brown will resist that pressure," said Stephen Yorke, director of political research at SBC Warburg.

He believes Brown will not want to be rushed into a decision so soon after taking office and that he may be planning a more ambitious mini-budget during his first two months in office than most people anticipate.
"I think it will be a radical budget. In terms of fiddling around on different tax measures and the rebalancing of the tax structure, it will do quite a lot," Yorke said.
